prompts.label: Check my design — no code
prompts.text: I believe backtracking with factors kept in non-decreasing order — each step tries f from the last factor up to sqrt(remaining) — so every combination is produced exactly once with no deduplication. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?

prompts.label: Review, do not rewrite
prompts.text: Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it.

prompts.label: Race conditions
prompts.text: Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Combinations concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet.

prompts.label: Tests that expose bugs
prompts.text: Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct.

prompts.label: Complexity check
prompts.text: What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Return **every way to write `n` as a product of two or more integers greater than 1** (`n` itself does not count). Each combination in non-decreasing order.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Does n itself count as a combination? (No.)
- Order inside a combination? (Non-decreasing.)
- Order of the list? (As generated: by first factor, then depth-first.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Duplicates like [2,6] and [6,2] disappear if factors may never decrease. Then only try factors up to the square root of what is left — anything bigger would have to be paired with something smaller, which you already tried.

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Generating permutations and deduplicating with a set.
- Trying factors up to n instead of sqrt(n).
- int overflow in f * f for large n.
- Including [n].
